q: Explain the effect of cyanide on sap flow.
Cyanide stops aerobic respiration, so there is no ATP for active transport of mineral ions into the xylem.
Use the solute concentrations to explain how root pressure is produced.

Root cells actively pump ions into the xylem (40 mmol dm⁻³ against 8 without ATP). This lowers the water potential of the xylem sap, so water enters by osmosis, building up pressure that pushes sap up the stem.
Explain why no sap flows when the soil water is very salty, even though the sap solutes are high.
The soil water now has an equal or lower water potential than the root cells, so water no longer enters the root by osmosis.
Explain the effect of low temperature.
Respiration and active transport are enzyme-driven and slow at 4 °C, so fewer ions are pumped and less water follows.
Suggest when root pressure is most important to a plant.
In spring (or at night), before leaves open and transpiration pull is weak: it refills the xylem.

18.t: Working with data: a tracer experiment
q: Identify the main sinks in the intact plant.
The developing pods and the roots.
Explain why other mature leaves receive almost none of the labelled carbon.
Mature leaves are sources themselves: they make their own sugar, so sucrose flows from them, not into them.
Describe and explain the effect of removing the ring of bark.

No label reached the roots, and more stayed in the leaf and went to the pods. Removing the bark removes the phloem, so sucrose cannot pass down the stem; the xylem is untouched, so water still reaches the leaves.
Explain how sucrose is loaded into the phloem and moved to a sink.

Companion cells load sucrose by active transport (proton co-transport). Water follows by osmosis, raising the hydrostatic pressure, so sap flows by mass flow towards the sink, where sucrose is removed and pressure is lower.
